title: Written information security program, scope and governance
status_rationale: No adopted security program charter, board resolution or program document was located. The only security policy artifact is the proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1, which explicitly says formal adoption is not established. Echelon Foundry, LLC is under formation.
target_answer: Echelon maintains a written information security program approved by its managing member(s) or board, scoped to Echelon Foundry, LLC, all Echelon products (including Unbound), all personnel, contractors and the AI agents that perform engineering and operations work. The program is aligned primarily to NIST CSF 2.0 with control mappings to SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria and ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A, is reviewed at least annually and on material change, and tracks regulatory change for the customer segments served (GLBA Safeguards, NYDFS Part 500 for New York covered entities, FFIEC guidance for banks). Program records, control register and evidence are machine-readable and versioned.
current_practice: Unknown; no evidence located of an adopted program charter. A proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1 exists (echelon-organization-administration@2763e576:policies/security/secure-construction-standard.md). The Unbound repository contains a SOC 2 readiness directive and a designed control matrix whose controls are all status Designed with no operating evidence.
intended_practice: Adopt a program charter and policy set by formal resolution of the LLC's governing body, then operate the Unbound control register as the program's control inventory.
provable: Nothing for an operating program. The existence of the proposed standard and the designed (not operating) Unbound control matrix can be shown.
customer_statement: Echelon has not yet adopted a formal information security program. A proposed Secure Construction Standard (v0.1) and a designed control framework for Unbound exist; formal adoption and operation are planned before any production service.
residual_risks: A small organization may adopt a program on paper that it lacks staff to operate.
open_questions: Who is the governing body of Echelon Foundry, LLC that would formally adopt the program?
Is Echelon itself a financial institution under the FTC Safeguards Rule because of activities described in UNB-XIN-REG-002, independent of its customers' status?

title: Security leadership: CISO or qualified individual, independence and succession
status_rationale: No named security officer, CISO, qualified individual or security staff is established in any reviewed record. The current-state brief forbids claiming a named security officer.
target_answer: Echelon designates a qualified individual (CISO or equivalent, which may be a contracted fractional CISO with documented oversight) who owns the program, reports in writing at least annually to the governing body, has direct access to the governing body and to sponsor audit and risk committees where contracts require it, can block a release on security grounds through the mandatory release gates, and has a documented deputy for incident periods.
current_practice: Unknown; no evidence located. Unbound requirements state the target that the CISO has a direct reporting line to the audit and risk committee (TVR-ORG-006) and direct access to it (CNV-GOV-003), but these are requirements for the Unbound operating model, not evidence of an appointment.
intended_practice: Appoint a qualified individual before onboarding any customer data; record the appointment, qualifications, reporting line and deputy; give the role release-blocking authority through Praxis gates.
customer_statement: Echelon has not yet appointed a CISO or qualified individual. Appointment, reporting line and deputy arrangements will be documented before any customer data is processed.
residual_risks: A fractional or combined role (for example CTO and CISO) concentrates authority and may weaken independence.
Key-person dependency in a very small organization.
open_questions: Will Echelon use a fractional CISO, and if so which firm and with what oversight by a senior Echelon member (16 CFR 314.4(a) allows a service-provider qualified individual with oversight)?

challenge.customer_intent: Ensure a single accountable, competent person owns security and can stand up to commercial pressure.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Security decisions are made by nobody or by people with conflicting incentives; incidents lack leadership.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: A named CISO is a necessary accountability anchor but does not by itself produce secure systems; effectiveness depends on authority, budget and staff that a startup may lack.
challenge.legally_required: For customers that are covered entities, NYDFS 23 NYCRR 500.4 and the FTC Safeguards Rule 16 CFR 314.4(a) require the customer to designate a CISO or qualified individual; they do not directly require the vendor to have one, but customers routinely flow the expectation down.
challenge.contractually_required: Common in bank and wealth-manager vendor questionnaires and security addenda.
challenge.historical_convention: Strong convention; examiners and third-party risk teams expect a named security leader at each critical vendor.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Not eliminable. Architecture can reduce the scope of decisions a CISO must make by hand (fail-closed gates, structural rules), but accountability cannot be engineered away.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Release-blocking authority can be implemented as a required approval role in the Praxis release gate rather than as an informal veto.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Gate decisions, exceptions approved and program reports can be generated continuously with attribution.
challenge.stronger_alternative: A fractional CISO with a contract that names the person, deputy, hours and escalation rights, combined with structural controls and continuous evidence, plus customer-visible gate records.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Partially: the appointment and gate records are verifiable; competence and attention are not.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If no person with security authority exists, no amount of automated evidence substitutes; if the fractional CISO cannot be reached during incidents.
challenge.conventional_cost: A full-time CISO is a large fixed cost for an early-stage company.
challenge.alternative_cost: Fractional CISO retainer plus engineering effort for gates; order-of-magnitude lower than full-time.
challenge.alternative_risks: Divided attention, weaker institutional knowledge, contract termination risk.
supporting_arguments: Regulations permit service-provider qualified individuals with oversight.
Structural controls reduce reliance on individual vigilance.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'A fractional CISO is generally acceptable to mid-market buyers and many community banks if named and contracted; large banks may ask about depth of bench.'; institutional acceptance rating 'uncertain' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Examiners may view a fractional CISO at a critical vendor as a concentration and depth risk.
Automated gates are only as good as the person who defines and maintains the rules.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Security policy set: content, approval, review and communication
status_rationale: The Secure Construction Standard v0.1 is a proposed organizational standard; implementation and external acceptance are explicitly not verified. No other security policies (acceptable use, access control, incident response, etc.) were located.
target_answer: Echelon maintains a complete, versioned policy set (information security, acceptable use, access control, secure construction, cryptography, change management, incident response, vendor management, data classification and retention, business continuity, AI agent operations), each with an owner, approval record, effective date and annual review. Policies are written as stable rule identifiers (for example SEC-AUTH-001) so that each rule maps to an enforcement mechanism, negative tests and evidence. Mandatory rules are enforced by fail-closed build and release gates; agent operating instructions (AGENTS.md) reference the same rule identifiers. Personnel and contractors acknowledge policies at onboarding and on material change.
current_practice: A proposed Secure Construction Standard v0.1 with ten rule identifiers exists (echelon-organization-administration@2763e576:policies/security/secure-construction-standard.md). Agent operating instructions exist in Echelon repositories (AGENTS.md), but they govern repository work procedure, not security policy. No acknowledgment records exist.
intended_practice: Formally adopt the standard and author the remaining policies with rule identifiers mapped to enforcement and evidence.
provable: The text of the proposed standard and its commit can be shown. Nothing proves adoption or enforcement.
customer_statement: Echelon has a proposed Secure Construction Standard (v0.1). It has not been formally adopted, and the remaining policy set is planned. Echelon intends every mandatory rule to have a stable identifier, an enforcement mechanism and evidence.
owner: Unassigned; proposed CISO or qualified individual
residual_risks: Policies written as enforceable rules may omit concerns that cannot be enforced in code (for example personnel conduct).
open_questions: Which body formally adopts policies and what is the approval artifact?

title: Policy exceptions and risk acceptance
status_rationale: The Secure Construction Standard requires explicit, narrowly scoped, time-limited, approved exceptions with compensating controls and no silent bypasses; SOC2-033 requires an exception register. Neither is implemented.
target_answer: Every exception to a mandatory rule is a recorded, versioned object with scope, rationale, compensating controls, approver (who cannot be the requester), expiry and linked evidence. Build and release gates read the exception register; an expired exception fails the gate automatically. Risk acceptance authority is defined by risk tier. There is no mechanism, for humans or AI agents, to bypass a mandatory gate without creating such a record, and the count and age of open exceptions are reported to leadership and, in summary, to customers.
current_practice: Unknown; no exception register exists. The proposed standard states the rule.
intended_practice: Implement an exception register consumed by Praxis gates; report exception counts in program metrics.
customer_statement: Echelon's proposed standard requires explicit, time-limited, approved exceptions with compensating controls and prohibits silent bypasses. An exception register enforced by build and release gates is planned.
owner: Unassigned; proposed CISO or qualified individual
residual_risks: An administrator with repository or pipeline administration rights could disable a gate outside the register; this requires separate change control and monitoring.

title: Security metrics and control effectiveness reporting
status_rationale: SOC2-034 defines objective coverage metrics and the continuous control monitoring architecture is specified, but nothing is implemented or operating.
target_answer: Echelon reports control effectiveness metrics generated from the control register and evidence stream: controls with owners, evidence emitted on schedule, missed runs, evidence integrity failures, overdue access reviews, open exceptions and their age, remediation aging by severity, negative-test pass rates for mandatory rules and tested effectiveness. Each metric carries its population definition, query, run log and hash (information produced by entity support) so a reviewer can verify completeness. A customer-facing summary is published monthly; detail is available under NDA.
current_practice: Unknown; no metrics are produced. Requirements exist in the Unbound repository (SOC2-034, CNV-GOV-001 on IPE support).
intended_practice: Build the metric set from the control register once controls operate; publish a monthly continuous assurance summary as the Secure Construction Standard proposes.
customer_statement: Echelon plans to report control effectiveness metrics generated from its control register, with population counts and query provenance so they can be independently checked. No metrics are produced today because no production service operates.
residual_risks: Automated metrics measure what is instrumented; uninstrumented controls look healthy by omission unless missing evidence is itself an exception (SOC2-027).

challenge.customer_intent: Know whether the vendor's security is working now, not only at the last audit.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Controls degrade between annual reviews without anyone noticing.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Point-in-time questionnaires and annual reports are stale on arrival and rely on self-assessment; SOC 2 Type 2 samples operation over a period but reports months later.
challenge.legally_required: No statute requires the vendor to publish metrics; customers' own oversight duties (Interagency TPRM guidance) require ongoing monitoring of critical vendors.
challenge.contractually_required: Some bank contracts require periodic security reporting; most rely on annual SOC reports.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Not applicable; this is a monitoring function.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Missing evidence can raise a control exception automatically.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Metrics can be regenerated on demand from signed evidence with population counts.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Continuous, signed control evidence with information-produced-by-entity support, exposed through a trust portal, supplemented by periodic independent attestation.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Verifiable for completeness and integrity if the query, population and hashes are provided; the correctness of the control logic still needs independent testing.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If the evidence pipeline is controlled by the same people whose controls it measures without independent review, it is self-assessment with better formatting.
challenge.conventional_cost: Annual questionnaire effort plus audit fees.
challenge.alternative_cost: Engineering investment in evidence generation; lower marginal cost per customer once built.
challenge.alternative_risks: Over-disclosure of exploitable detail; false confidence from green dashboards.
supporting_arguments: Generated evidence reduces audit preparation effort and staleness.
Population counts and hashes address completeness, a common audit weakness.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Buyers welcome continuous evidence as a supplement; few will accept it in place of a SOC report or examination-ready documentation.'; institutional acceptance rating 'uncertain' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: First-party dashboards are not independent assurance.
Auditors must still evaluate the design and the information produced by the entity.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Security awareness and role-based training
status_rationale: No training program, content, completion records or phishing exercises were located. No workforce headcount is established.
target_answer: All personnel and contractors complete security awareness training at onboarding and annually, with completion tracked and access suspended automatically when overdue. Role-based training covers secure construction for engineers, privileged access for administrators, and social engineering of support staff, including fraudulent payee, contact-detail and authenticator-reset requests and business email compromise patterns common in DAF and wealth-management operations. Because phishing-resistant authentication and structural controls remove many click-to-compromise paths, simulations focus on support-channel manipulation and approval fraud rather than credential capture.
intended_practice: Select a training provider or build role-specific modules; integrate completion with access provisioning.
customer_statement: Echelon does not yet operate a security awareness program. Onboarding and annual training with tracked completion, plus role-based training for engineering, administration and support, is planned before any customer data is processed.
owner: Unassigned; proposed CISO or qualified individual
residual_risks: Training cannot prevent determined social engineering of a small team; structural controls (dual control, cooling-off periods) are the primary defense.

challenge.customer_intent: Reduce the chance that a person is tricked into giving an attacker access or moving money.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Credential phishing, support-desk social engineering, or fraudulent payment and payee changes.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Annual awareness training and click-rate phishing simulations have limited and contested measured effect on breach likelihood; click rates are easy to report but weakly linked to outcomes.
challenge.legally_required: Required for the customer by FTC Safeguards Rule 16 CFR 314.4(e) and NYDFS 500.14 where they apply; customers flow the expectation to vendors contractually.
challenge.contractually_required: Nearly universal in bank and enterprise questionnaires.
challenge.historical_convention: Very strong; completion certificates are standard evidence.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Phishing-resistant authenticators (FIDO2/WebAuthn) eliminate credential replay from phishing in scope; help-desk resets, payee changes and authority changes can require dual control and cooling-off periods that do not depend on the staff member recognizing the attack.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Training completion can gate access; structural controls enforce independent of training.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Completion and access-suspension events are automatically recorded.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Keep baseline training for compliance, but invest primarily in structural controls: phishing-resistant MFA, no support-initiated authenticator resets without step-up, dual control on payee changes.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes; authenticator types and dual-control enforcement can be shown in configuration and tested.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If any user population still uses phishable factors or any support path can bypass dual control.
challenge.alternative_cost: Moderate engineering cost for structural controls, largely already required by Unbound requirements.
challenge.alternative_risks: Over-reliance on technology may neglect novel social engineering such as deepfake voice.
supporting_arguments: Phishing-resistant authentication removes the largest class of phishing harm.
Dual control and cooling-off periods work even when the person is fooled.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Customers will still require training evidence; structural controls are an addition, not a replacement, in their eyes.'; institutional acceptance rating 'unlikely' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Regulated customers must document vendor training regardless of effectiveness debates.
Some social engineering targets judgment calls no control can fully structure.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: AI agents within the security program (agentic engineering and operations)
status_rationale: Echelon repositories are worked on by AI coding agents and use Praxis to record self-declared actor attribution. Unbound requirements define agent authority tiers and tool-broker enforcement (UNB-AGT-003), but no production agent governance exists.
target_answer: Echelon discloses that AI agents perform engineering and some operations work. Agents are treated as workload identities under a named human owner; they operate only within repositories and environments whose mandatory rules are enforced by fail-closed gates rather than by prompt instructions; their contributions are attributed by execution identity and reviewed under the same two-approver rules as human changes for control-relevant modules (CNV-PLT-010). Agents never hold production credentials for customer data. Echelon discloses the model providers used in development and in the product, and agent instructions reference the same security rule identifiers as human policy.
current_practice: Praxis (praxis@12bf9951) records actor kind, provider, model and runtime per execution in Echelon repositories; attribution is self-declared from environment variables and flags and is not cryptographically authenticated (docs/agent-provenance.md). Production agent governance does not exist because no production service exists.
intended_practice: Bind agent executions to authenticated workload identities in CI; enforce rules through gates; publish a model-provider disclosure.
provable: Praxis execution and provenance records in development repositories show which actor kind and declared model produced a change. They do not prove the declared identity is true.
customer_statement: Echelon uses AI agents in engineering. Its Praxis tool records self-declared attribution of agent work in development repositories; this is not authenticated identity. Platform-enforced agent controls and a model-provider disclosure are planned for production.
owner: Unassigned; proposed CISO with AI governance owner
residual_risks: Self-declared agent attribution can be spoofed by any process able to set environment variables.
Model providers may change model behavior without notice.
open_questions: Which model providers process Echelon source code or customer data, and under what data-use terms?

challenge.customer_intent: Ensure that work performed by AI agents is as controlled and accountable as work by employees.
challenge.adverse_outcome: An agent introduces a vulnerability, exfiltrates data, or takes an unauthorized action with no accountable human.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Conventional controls (training, acceptable-use acknowledgment, background checks) do not apply to agents at all.
challenge.legally_required: No US statute specifically regulates vendor use of AI coding agents; EU AI Act obligations depend on the system's risk classification and are not established here.
challenge.contractually_required: Emerging; some enterprise contracts now restrict AI processing of customer data or require disclosure.
challenge.historical_convention: None established; questionnaires are adding AI sections.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Agents can be denied production credentials entirely and confined to repositories where every change passes the same gates as human changes.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Tool brokers remove prohibited tools rather than instructing agents not to use them (UNB-AGT-003); gates enforce rules regardless of author.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Execution identity and per-change provenance are generated by construction.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Treat every agent as an untrusted contributor whose output must pass structural gates and human approval for control-relevant modules, with authenticated workload identity in CI.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Gate results and approvals are verifiable; agent identity is only verifiable once bound to authenticated workload credentials.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If agents can push to protected branches, hold production secrets, or self-approve.
challenge.alternative_cost: Moderate; largely tooling Echelon already builds.
challenge.alternative_risks: Review fatigue from high agent output volume may degrade human approval quality.
supporting_arguments: Agents cannot be socially engineered in the same way, but can be prompt-injected; gates address both.
Provenance by construction exceeds what most vendors record about human contributors.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Uncertain; some regulated buyers are uneasy about AI-written code in financial systems regardless of controls.'; institutional acceptance rating 'uncertain' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Self-declared attribution is not identity assurance.
Human reviewers may rubber-stamp large agent-generated changes.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Independent review of the security program and assurance labeling
status_rationale: No external assessment, internal audit, SOC report, ISO certificate or penetration test exists. The Secure Construction Standard requires first-party reports to be labeled as such.
target_answer: Echelon obtains independent assurance appropriate to customer reliance: a SOC 2 Type 2 (and SOC 1 Type 2 where a sponsor's auditor relies on Unbound controls, per CNV-GOV-001) and periodic independent program assessment. All first-party assessments and automated evidence are labeled first-party and never presented as independent. Customers and their examiners may assess the program under contractual audit rights with reasonable notice.
current_practice: No independent review has occurred. Requirements for labeling (Secure Construction Standard) and for assurance scope (CNV-GOV-001) exist as proposals.
intended_practice: Plan assurance scope from actual customer reliance; label all internal evidence as first-party.
provable: Nothing independent. The proposed labeling rule can be shown.
customer_statement: Echelon has no independent security assessment, SOC report or certification today. Independent assurance will be scoped to customer reliance before production use, and all internal evidence will be labeled first-party.
owner: Unassigned; proposed CISO or qualified individual
residual_risks: Independent assurance is periodic and scoped; it does not cover everything customers assume.
